subject: physics
title: Electricity & Magnetism Adventure 1: Coulomb's law and electric fields
welcome_lead: Today you'll feel Coulomb's force and map electric fields.
meta_desc: Physics — Coulomb's law, electric field E, potential V, parallel plates.
final_note: You learned F = kq₁q₂/r², E = F/q, V = work/q, between parallel plates E = V/d.

walkthroughs.body_html:
F = k · q₁ · q₂ / r²

k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m²/C².
Same sign → repulsion. Opposite → attraction.

1 C is a huge charge: two 1 C charges 1 m apart push with 9 × 10⁹ N. Realistic charges are nC or μC.

E = F/q (N/C). Field lines from + to −.

Point charge: E = kQ/r².

Electric potential V (scalar): work done per unit charge from infinity. V = kQ/r for point.

Equipotentials ⊥ field lines.

Uniform field between plates: E = V/d.

V volts, d metres, E in V/m.

Cathode ray tube: deflect electron beam.
Capacitor stores energy ½ CV² (HL).

Lightning: huge V between cloud and ground; air dielectric breaks down at ~3 × 10⁶ V/m.

Is radioactive decay periodic — does each nucleus decay at regular intervals?
options: Low-frequency light doesn't have enough mass to push electrons out of the metal.
Yes — each nucleus 'ticks' at intervals of one half-life until it decays.
No — decay is a random process; half-life is a statistical property of a large population.
Yes — half-life is the time between each emission from the source.

mcqs.q: Why does increasing the intensity of light below the threshold frequency not eject electrons?
options: Each photon's energy is below the work function; many low-energy photons can't combine to eject an electron.
Yes — half-life is the time between each emission from the source.
Low-frequency light doesn't have enough mass to push electrons out of the metal.
Enough low-frequency photons should eventually eject an electron if you wait long enough.

mcqs.q: Is ultraviolet light visible to humans?
options: No — even though it sits next to violet on the spectrum, its frequency is above the range our eyes detect.
Yes — UV is visible because it's right next to violet.
Yes — UV is the colour purple.
Yes — half-life is the time between each emission from the source.
